quarterly_data.signal: Q2 2026 revenue by end market (CEO Haviv Ilan): industrial increased around 30% year-over-year and about 10% sequentially, growing broadly across sectors and regions; automotive increased in the mid-teens year-on-year and upper single digits sequentially; data center doubled year-on-year and grew around 20% sequentially; personal electronics was flat year-on-year and grew upper single digits sequentially; communications equipment grew both year-on-year and sequentially. Revenue came in above the range. CFO Rafael Lizardi: gross profit margin increased 340 basis points sequentially; trailing 12-month operating expenses were $3.9 billion, or 20% of revenue; trailing 12-month free cash flow includes $1.6 billion of CHIPS Act incentives (investment tax credit and direct funding).
quarterly_data.figure: industrial around +30% YoY; automotive mid-teens YoY; data center doubled YoY (around +20% sequentially); personal electronics flat YoY

quarterly_data.signal: Demand outlook (CEO Haviv Ilan): 'we see a setup of a stronger demand; it's broader' - the above-seasonal Q3 guide draws on all markets. Automotive demand built up through the quarter, led by China and by EVs and hybrids (he believes the cost of fuel drove that), and automotive customers had taken inventory to very low levels: 'I think we are in the start of a cycle that is very broad.' Industrial is still maybe five or six points below its 2022 peak against a mid- to high single-digit trend-line growth; energy infrastructure and test and measurement were the fastest-growing sectors in the first half, the data center is providing a tailwind into industrial, and customers 'have not yet built inventory'. IR head Mike Beckman: aerospace and defense, energy infrastructure and robotics grew at higher rates, every sector and region grew, and he attributes it more to secular content growth than pricing. Personal electronics is expected to grow sequentially in Q3 but at a lower level than its typical Q3 growth (sometimes mid-teens), as shortages are putting pressure on customers. Backlog built throughout Q2, both in orders for immediate shipment and in backlog further out. CEO: TI picked some market share last year, and competitors quoting lead times 52 weeks away are an opportunity as customers sometimes start new designs.

Data center (CEO Haviv Ilan): strong demand that he does not expect to change in the foreseeable future. 800-volt architectures will be phased in - e.g. AC to 800 volts, then 800 volts to 48 volts to 12 volts - meaning higher TAM growth and more conversion stages, with analog parts in every conversion stage plus embedded controllers and signal-chain parts; longer term, once the SST is established, data center input will be 800 volts DC with possibly direct conversion from 800 directly to 12 or six volts: 'The higher voltage, the more opportunity we see.' Customers come with real-time 'we are lined down; please help us' requests that TI meets from inventory and capacity, 'part of the reason why you've seen our business doubling, more or less year to date'; TI plans to keep capacity and clean room inventory ahead of demand. Supply from 'geopolitically dependable capacity' is becoming an advantage; the objective is to outgrow the market in 2026 and into 2027. IR head Mike Beckman: TI chips sit across the data center power tree and signal chain, with ASSP opportunities on top; data center gross margin has so far been pretty similar to the corporate average, and the ramp is on 300mm newer assets.
quarterly_data.figure: data center doubled YoY; 800 volts to 48 volts to 12 volts conversion stages

quarterly_data.signal: Pricing and lead times (CEO Haviv Ilan): pricing was stable - flat - in the first half, versus the usual decline of a couple of points a year. 'I will say that we have started executing price increases, yes' - customer by customer since TI goes to market direct; some will start to play in Q3 and he expects it to continue into the fourth quarter, with annual price discussions at the end of Q4 continuing into next year. Pressure and lead-time escalation are mainly on the analog side (automotive cited); embedded is joining the trend, with embedded pricing discussions centred on next year. For the Q3 forecast, 'the vast majority of it is just unit growth', with the pricing contribution 'almost insignificant'. Lead times were below 13 weeks in Q2 with 'a little bit of an uptick', maybe a couple of weeks higher, because demand is growing; he believes TI's lead times are the most competitive in the market.
quarterly_data.figure: first-half pricing flat; price increases starting in Q3; lead times below 13 weeks, maybe a couple of weeks higher

quarterly_data.signal: Capacity and loadings: incoming CFO Julie Knecht said factory loadings increased from Q1 to Q2 and continued to increase throughout Q2; Q3 loadings depend on demand, with clean room space available to equip. CEO Haviv Ilan: TI is equipping Richardson RFAB2 at a very high level, has a full clean room 'available almost in Sherman 1' plus a second shell in Sherman 2; Lehi 2 - needed as embedded growth picks up after Lehi 1 absorbed the transfer of Stellaris manufacturing from foundries - will have its shell at the end of this year, with no new customer qualifications needed. 'In general, we are good for the next three years' on clean rooms (phase three: modulate the equipment). Inventory ended Q2 at $4.6 billion, down $90 million from the prior quarter, at 196 days (down 13 days sequentially).
quarterly_data.figure: inventory $4.6 billion, 196 days (down 13 days); clean room capacity good for the next three years

quarterly_data.signal: Outlook detail from the call, beyond the Q3 revenue ($5.65 billion-$6.15 billion) and EPS ($2.23-$2.57) ranges: Q3 effective tax rate about 13%; operating expenses, net other income and expense and acquisition charges flat from Q2 (CFO Rafael Lizardi); fall-through of 70%-85% excluding depreciation is a good placeholder (Julie Knecht), with gross margin 'a little higher' rather than flat (Lizardi). 2026 capex 'continues to be $2 billion-$3 billion' - 'If anything, it could be on the higher end of that midpoint, just given demand'; future capex will be disproportionately in assembly test operations outside the U.S., which do not get the investment tax credit, while TI continues to get 35% ITC on U.S. front-end manufacturing, which can be choppy. Capital intensity rule of thumb stays 1.2x the growth; 2027 capex numbers will come at the capital management call in February. CEO Haviv Ilan: the free cash flow framework is still valid - $8 billion-$9 billion at $20 billion of revenue and $9 billion-$10 billion at $22 billion.
quarterly_data.figure: Q3 tax rate about 13%; 2026 capex $2 billion-$3 billion; free cash flow framework $8 billion-$9 billion at $20 billion revenue

quarterly_data.signal: Pending acquisition of Silicon Labs (incoming CFO Julie Knecht): regulatory approvals are moving as planned, and TI still expects to close in the first half of next year.
